title: Letters to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea
summary: The risen Christ addresses the last three churches. Sardis has a reputation for being alive but is dead, and is told to wake up. Philadelphia has little strength but has kept Christ's word, and he sets before it an open door and promises to keep it in the hour of trial. Laodicea is lukewarm and self-satisfied, thinking itself rich while it is poor, blind, and naked. Christ counsels it to buy true wealth from him, and he stands at the door and knocks.
story: Chapter 3 completes the seven messages begun in chapter 2. Of the seven churches, only Smyrna and Philadelphia receive no rebuke, and the two most severely warned, Sardis and Laodicea, are the ones that seem outwardly comfortable. With Laodicea the messages end and the scene shifts: in chapter 4 John sees a door standing open in heaven and is shown the throne of God. The promise that the overcomer will sit with Christ on his throne (3:21) leads straight into that throne-room vision, where the one who overcame appears as the slain Lamb.
historical:
Sardis had been the capital of the kingdom of Lydia, whose king Croesus was proverbial for wealth, and the Lydians are credited with some of the first coins. Its citadel stood on a steep hill and was thought impregnable, yet it fell by surprise to the Persian king Cyrus around 546 BC, when soldiers climbed an unguarded slope, and again to the Seleucid king Antiochus III in 214 BC. Many commentators connect that history with Christ's warning: wake up, or I will come like a thief. In AD 17 a great earthquake devastated Sardis and other cities of the region, and the emperor Tiberius helped rebuild them.

Philadelphia, the youngest of the seven cities, was founded in the second century BC by the kings of Pergamum and named for the brotherly love (philadelphia) between King Attalus II and his brother Eumenes II. It stood at the edge of the fertile plain that led east into Phrygia. It suffered severely in the earthquake of AD 17 and in ongoing tremors; the geographer Strabo wrote that many of its people lived outside the city for fear of falling walls. In gratitude for imperial help it took the name Neocaesarea, and later, under Vespasian, it was also called Flavia. The promises of a pillar that will never have to leave and of a new name have been read against that background.

Laodicea, in the Lycus valley about a hundred miles east of Ephesus, was a wealthy center of banking, of a glossy black wool, and of medicine; a medical school was associated with the area, and an eye remedy known as Phrygian powder was famous in the ancient world. After an earthquake in AD 60, the historian Tacitus records that Laodicea rebuilt from its own resources without help from Rome. Paul's letter to the Colossians mentions the church there (Colossians 4:13-16).
cultural:
Laodicea had no good water supply of its own and brought water by an aqueduct from springs several miles away. By the time it arrived, it was lukewarm, and its heavy mineral content left thick deposits in the pipes. Nearby Hierapolis was known for its hot springs, used for healing, and Colossae for cold, fresh water. Many interpreters think Christ's words play on this: hot water heals and cold water refreshes, but lukewarm water is useless and makes a person want to spit it out. On this reading, hot and cold are both good; the problem is uselessness, not a lack of enthusiasm. An older reading takes hot as spiritual zeal and cold as outright rejection, so that even open hostility would be better than indifference. The water background is widely accepted, though not universally.

The counsel to buy gold, white garments, and eye salve (verse 18) seems pointed at the city's pride in its banking, its black wool, and its eye medicine. Clothing also mattered in the letter to Sardis, whose faithful few have not soiled their garments. In the ancient world white robes were worn at festivals and victory celebrations, and the book of life (verse 5) recalls the citizen registers that cities kept, from which a name could be struck. The key of David (verse 7) comes from Isaiah 22:22, where authority over the royal household is given to a faithful steward, Eliakim.
literary: The three messages follow the pattern of chapter 2: a title of Christ, I know your deeds, commendation or rebuke, a call to repent or hold fast, a promise to the overcomer, and the refrain He who has an ear. Sardis receives almost no praise; Philadelphia receives no rebuke; Laodicea receives no praise at all. The letters are full of contrasts: alive and dead, little strength and an open door, rich and poor, clothed and naked. The image of the door runs through the chapter, from the open door no one can shut at Philadelphia (verse 8) to the door where Christ knocks at Laodicea (verse 20), and on into chapter 4's door opened in heaven. The Laodicean letter includes the church's own words, quoted back to it (verse 17), and then a tender turn: those I love, I rebuke and discipline.

outline.t: Sardis: a reputation for life, but dead
Philadelphia: little strength, an open door
Laodicea: lukewarm, and Christ at the door

doctrines.note: Sardis is told to wake up, remember, and repent; Laodicea to be earnest and repent. Christ's rebuke is an act of love, and the door to renewal stays open to any who hear his voice (verses 19-20).
A church can have a good reputation and be dead, or be weak and faithful. Christ judges by what he sees, not by how the church sees itself. His knowledge of each church is exact and loving.

The overcomer will be dressed in white, never blotted from the book of life, made a pillar in God's temple, inscribed with the name of the new Jerusalem, and seated with Christ on his throne. These promises anticipate the final chapters of the book.
Laodicea's sin is self-sufficiency: I am rich and need nothing. Wealth and comfort become idols when they persuade a church that it no longer needs Christ.

words.note: Chliaros, lukewarm, found only here in the New Testament. It describes water that is neither hot nor cold. Given Laodicea's piped water, the word probably pictures a church that neither heals nor refreshes, and whose self-satisfaction has made it useless to its Lord.

Thyra, door, used three times in the chapter. At Philadelphia Christ sets an open door no one can shut, probably an opportunity for witness or entrance into his kingdom. At Laodicea he stands outside the church's own door and knocks, asking to come in and share a meal.

Arche, beginning, origin, or ruler. Christ calls himself the Originator (arche) of God's creation (verse 14). The word can mean the first in a series, but here it is best read as the source or ruler of creation, echoing Colossians 1:15-18, a letter also read at Laodicea.

christ: Christ presents himself in this chapter as the one who holds the seven Spirits and the seven stars, the holy and true one who holds the key of David, and the Amen, the faithful and true Witness, the Originator of God's creation. Each title claims divine authority: the key of David makes him the true king over God's household, and Amen, a word used of God in Isaiah 65:16, makes him the final guarantee of God's promises. Yet the most famous image of the chapter is humble: the Lord of creation standing at the door of a lukewarm church and knocking, offering to come in and eat with anyone who opens. His discipline flows from love (verse 19), and his last promise is to share his own throne with those who overcome as he overcame.

hard.q: Does the promise to keep Philadelphia from the hour of testing mean the church will be taken out of the world before a great tribulation?
hard.a:
Verse 10 is a key text in the debate over the timing of the rapture, the gathering of believers to meet Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Pretribulationists, especially within dispensational premillennialism, read keep you from the hour as a promise of removal from the period of trial itself, which they identify with a future seven-year tribulation. They note that the hour of testing comes upon the whole world, not only Philadelphia. Posttribulationists and many others read it as a promise of protection through the trial rather than removal from it, and they point to Jesus' prayer in John 17:15, which uses the same verb and preposition: not to take them out of the world but to keep them from the evil one. Amillennial and preterist readers often see the hour of testing as a trial in the first century or as the recurring trials of the whole church age.

Each view is held by faithful Christians. What the verse plainly offers the small, weak church at Philadelphia is Christ's own commitment: because they kept his word, he will keep them. The next verse calls them to hold fast, whatever the hour brings.

questions: Sardis had a reputation for being alive but was dead. How would you know if your own faith or church were living on a reputation?
Philadelphia had only a little strength but kept Christ's word. Where does weakness make you think you have nothing to offer, and what open door might Christ be setting before you?
Laodicea said, I need nothing. In what areas of your life has comfort made you forget your need of Christ, and what would it mean to open the door?
